text: There are more than ten thousand active satellites in orbit
as_written: More than ten thousand active satellites circle the Earth
source: Jonathan McDowell's satellite catalogue and the Union of Concerned Scientists Satellite Database

text: A low orbit satellite at about 550 km travels at about 7.6 km/s
as_written: At around five hundred and fifty kilometres up, a typical low orbit satellite is travelling at about seven and a half kilometres per second
source: Circular orbital velocity from Newtonian mechanics, v = sqrt(GM/r), with Earth's standard gravitational parameter (IERS/IAU)

text: Low orbit satellites circle the Earth roughly every ninety minutes
as_written: roughly every ninety minutes
source: Kepler's third law applied to a ~550 km orbit; NASA orbital mechanics references

text: The GPS constellation has about thirty operational satellites
as_written: number about thirty
source: GPS.gov constellation status, US Space Force / National Coordination Office for Space-Based PNT

text: GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km
as_written: roughly twenty thousand two hundred kilometres
source: GPS.gov, Space Segment description

text: Each GPS satellite orbits the Earth twice a day
as_written: each one circles the Earth twice a day
source: GPS.gov, Space Segment description (orbital period about 11 h 58 min)

text: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and broadcast time stamps
as_written: Each carries atomic clocks and broadcasts a time stamp
source: GPS.gov; GPS Interface Specification IS-GPS-200

text: A receiver needs four or more satellites to solve position and time
as_written: Your phone listens to four or more of them
source: GPS.gov, How GPS Works

text: Light travels about 30 cm in one nanosecond
as_written: light covers about thirty centimetres in one nanosecond
source: SI definition of the speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s (BIPM)

text: A one microsecond timing error corresponds to about 300 m of range error
as_written: an error of one microsecond ... becomes an error of about three hundred metres
source: Speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s (BIPM)

text: Geostationary orbit is 35,786 km above the equator
as_written: thirty five thousand seven hundred and eighty six kilometres above the equator
source: NASA and ESA orbital reference data

text: Many cellular systems require base station phase synchronisation within about 1.5 microseconds
as_written: within about one and a half microseconds of each other
source: ITU-T Recommendation G.8271 (time and phase synchronisation for packet networks)

text: European rules require high frequency trading timestamps accurate to within 100 microseconds of UTC
as_written: accurate to within one hundred microseconds of Coordinated Universal Time
source: MiFID II, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/574 (RTS 25)

text: A 2019 study for NIST estimated a GPS outage would cost the US economy about $1 billion per day on average, more in planting season
as_written: about one billion dollars per day on average, and more during planting season
source: RTI International, Economic Benefits of the Global Positioning System to the U.S. Private Sector, prepared for NIST, 2019

text: A UK study estimated a GPS outage would cost around one billion pounds per day
as_written: around one billion pounds per day
source: London Economics, The Economic Impact on the UK of a Disruption to GNSS, 2017

text: ECMWF relies mostly on satellite observations
as_written: the great majority of the observations it uses come from satellites
source: ECMWF, Observations and data assimilation documentation

text: GOES satellites are American geostationary weather satellites
as_written: the American GOES series
source: NOAA GOES-R Series Program

text: SpaceX reported well over 100,000 collision avoidance manoeuvres in a six month period
as_written: well over one hundred thousand avoidance manoeuvres in a single six month period
source: SpaceX Starlink semiannual constellation reports to the FCC (December 2024 to May 2025)

text: The Iridium 33 and Cosmos 2251 collision occurred in February 2009 at about 790 km altitude
as_written: In February two thousand nine ... at about seven hundred and ninety kilometres up
source: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, Orbital Debris Quarterly News

text: The closing speed of the 2009 collision was about 11.7 km/s
as_written: roughly eleven point seven kilometres per second
source: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office

text: The 2009 collision produced thousands of tracked fragments
as_written: thousands of tracked fragments
source: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office; US Space Surveillance Network

text: Kessler and Cour-Palais published the collision cascade concept in 1978
as_written: first described in nineteen seventy eight by two NASA scientists, Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais
source: Kessler and Cour-Palais, Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1978

text: About a million debris pieces between 1 and 10 cm exist
as_written: about a million pieces larger than one centimetre but smaller than ten
source: ESA Space Debris Office, Space Environment Report

text: About 130 million debris pieces between 1 mm and 1 cm exist
as_written: about one hundred and thirty million pieces between one millimetre and one centimetre
source: ESA Space Debris Office, Space Environment Report

text: China's 2007 anti-satellite test on Fengyun-1C created more than 3,000 trackable pieces
as_written: more than three thousand trackable pieces
source: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office

text: The November 2021 Russian test on Cosmos 1408 produced about 1,500 trackable fragments and ISS crew sheltered
as_written: about fifteen hundred trackable fragments, and the crew of the International Space Station had to shelter
source: US Space Command statement and NASA, November 2021

text: Coordinated Universal Time is computed by the BIPM from atomic clocks in national laboratories
as_written: calculated by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in France, using hundreds of atomic clocks held in dozens of national laboratories
source: BIPM Time Department, Circular T

text: About 99 percent of intercontinental data travels via undersea cables
as_written: Roughly ninety nine percent of intercontinental data travels through undersea cables
source: TeleGeography; International Cable Protection Committee

text: Uncontrolled geostationary satellites drift to about 15 degrees inclination over roughly 26 years
as_written: about fifteen degrees over roughly a quarter of a century
source: ESA Space Debris Office; Soop and others, Handbook of Geostationary Orbits

text: SpaceX says dead Starlink satellites at operating altitude reenter within a few years
as_written: burns up within a few years
source: SpaceX Starlink Gen2 orbital debris mitigation filings to the FCC

text: In February 2022 a geomagnetic storm caused 38 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites to be lost
as_written: a batch of forty nine Starlink satellites ... Thirty eight of them fell and burned up
source: SpaceX Updates, 'Geomagnetic Storm' post, February 2022

text: The May 2024 storm was rated G5, the strongest in about two decades
as_written: the strongest geomagnetic storm in two decades, rated G5
source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, May 2024 storm assessment

text: An international guideline says low orbit satellites should be removed within 25 years of mission end
as_written: within twenty five years of the end of their mission
source: Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC) Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines
